newsitem.title: USA: Albright, Estonia minister discuss NATO.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Estonia minister discuss NATO.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Estonian Foreign Minister Toomas Ilves on Thursday endorsed Estonia's right to press for NATO membership even if neighbouring Russia disapproves.

At the start of talks at the State Department, Albright also renewed U.S. assurances that Estonia's hopes to join NATO would not be foreclosed if it is not among the first group of members selected to join the organisation four months from now.
She stressed that the U.S. goal of an integrated Europe includes Estonia which has emerged from 50 years of Soviet domination as a "vibrant, prosperous and democratic success story."
She said she was aware that as NATO approaches its July summit in Madrid when new alliance members will be named "there is concern about which countries will be invited in the first round."

But reflecting an intense U.S. effort to provide reassurances at every opportunity, she stressed that even after Madrid "NATO will remain open to all European democracies that are able to contribute to its goal. This is fundamental."

The Washington Post reported Friday that the Clinton administration was offering to negotiate a security agreement with the three Baltic nations -- Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania -- in an attempt to ease their concerns.
Quoting unidentified U.S. officials and Baltic diplomats, the newspaper said the United States was drafting a bilateral charter setting out its future relationship with all three Baltic countries.
Top contenders for early NATO membership are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Romainia nd Slovenia are also under discussion.
Ilves dismissed the suggestion that Estonia may never be permitted to join the 16-member Western alliance and said he was not worried that Russia might find such membership threatening.
"I certainly do not believe that a country has to give up its aspirations to freely join an organisation simply because its neighbour objects," he told reporters at a brief news conference.

Albright agreed, saying: "I believe that it is important for the countries of Europe as well as Russia to understand the possibilities of countries to in fact choose which alliances they want to be in."
"The NATO process is an open one and the first countries accepted will not be the last," she said.
